hints: Focus on what atomisation really means, forming single, separate gaseous atoms starting from the element itself.
Remember chlorine exists as $\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)}$ in its standard state under standard conditions, and the definition needs exactly 1 mol of $\text{Cl(g)}$.
Check whether each equation makes one mole or two moles of gaseous atoms, since only one of them fits the per mole definition.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definition of atomisation**

Standard enthalpy of atomisation is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state.

Definition:
$$\text{element (standard state)} \rightarrow 1 \text{ mol of gaseous atoms}$$

**Identify the standard state of chlorine**

Chlorine is a gas at standard conditions, so we must start from $\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)}$, not $\text{Cl}_2\text{(l)}$.

That immediately rules out any equation starting with liquid chlorine.

**Fix the moles to make one atom**

We need exactly $1$ mol of $\text{Cl(g)}$ as product. Starting from $\text{Cl}_2$ means we need only half a molecule:
$$\frac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{Cl(g)}$$
This matches the definition perfectly, so this is the correct equation.

options.A: Correct. It starts from the standard state $\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)}$ and forms exactly 1 mol of $\text{Cl(g)}$. This is exactly the definition of standard enthalpy of atomisation.
options.B: Incorrect. Although it forms 1 mol of $\text{Cl(g)}$, it starts from $\text{Cl}_2\text{(l)}$. Chlorine is a gas in its standard state, so this includes an extra vaporisation step.
options.C: Incorrect. It has the correct states, $\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)}$ to $\text{Cl(g)}$, but it forms 2 mol of atoms. This is the bond dissociation enthalpy of $\text{Cl}_2$, which is twice the atomisation enthalpy.
options.D: Incorrect. It is wrong twice over. It starts from the wrong state $\text{Cl}_2\text{(l)}$ and it forms 2 mol of $\text{Cl(g)}$ instead of 1 mol.
